keyConcepts.text: Reading numbers involves interpreting them as a quantity when they are expressed in words, in standard notation, or represented using physical objects or diagrams.

The numerals 0 to 9 are used to form numbers. They are referred to as the digits in a number and each digit corresponds to a place value. For example, in the number 4107, the digit 4 represents 4 thousands, the digit 1 represents 1 hundred, the digit 0 represents 0 tens, and the digit 7 represents 7 ones.
There are patterns in the way numbers are formed. Each decade repeats the 0 to 9 counting sequence. Any quantity, no matter how great, can be described in terms of its place value.
A number can be represented in expanded form (e.g., 3187 = 3000 + 100 + 80 + 7 or 3 × 1000 + 1 × 100 + 8 × 10 + 7 × 1) to show place value relationships.
Numbers can be composed and decomposed in various ways, including by place value.
Numbers are composed when two or more numbers are combined to create a larger number. For example, 300, 200, and 6 combine to make 506.
Numbers are decomposed when they are represented as a composition of two or more smaller numbers. For example, 512 can be represented as 250 and 250 and 10 and 2.
Tools may be used when representing numbers. For example, 362 may be represented as the sum of 36 ten-dollar bills and 1 toonie or 3 base ten flats, 6 base ten rods, and 2 base ten units.

Numbers are used throughout the day, in various ways and contexts. Most often, numbers describe and compare quantities. They express magnitude and provide a way to answer questions such as “how much?” and “how much more?”.

tasks.text: Have students use an open number line to show various ways to reach a number, for example, 638, and record the sequence of jumps using an equation. Emphasize that all of these ways end at the same point – 638 – and that there are many different ways to make the same amount.
As students develop a familiarity with the various ways they can decompose a number, have them create clues to determine Which Number Am I?. For example:
items: My number has 6 ones, 8 hundreds, and 6 tens.
My number has 16 tens and 16 ones.
My number is greater than 450 but less than 580, has a zero in the tens place, and has 9 ones.

tasks.text: Have students visualize these quantities and use models such as a number line or base ten materials to verify their predictions.

Have students use base ten materials to represent a number, such as representing 647 using 6 flats, 4 rods, and 7 small cubes. Ask them to represent the number again in a different way by decomposing and composing their base ten representation. For example, they could exchange one of their flats for 10 rods, so their new representation would be 5 flats, 14 rods, and 7 small cubes. Draw out the connection between a digit’s place in a number and the value or quantity it represents.

keyConcepts.text: Numbers are compared and ordered according to their “how muchness” or magnitude.

Numbers with the same units can be compared directly (e.g., 645 days compared to 625 days). Numbers that do not show a unit are assumed to have units of ones (e.g., 75 and 12 are considered as 75 ones and 12 ones).

Sometimes numbers without the same unit can be compared, such as 625 weeks and 75 days. Knowing that the unit "weeks" is greater than the unit "days", and knowing that 625 is greater than 75, one can infer that 625 weeks is a greater length of time than 75 days.
Benchmark numbers can be used to compare quantities. For example, 132 is less than 500 and 620 is greater than 500, so 132 is less than 620.

Numbers can be compared by their place value. For example, when comparing 825 and 845, the greatest place value in which the numbers differ is compared. For this example, 2 tens (from 825) and 4 tens (from 845) are compared. Since 4 tens is greater than 2 tens, 845 is greater than 825.
Numbers can be ordered in ascending order – from least to greatest – or can be ordered in descending order – from greatest to least.

tasks.text: To strengthen understanding of place value and develop the skills needed to compare and order numbers, create a number line clothesline. Use clothespins to hang benchmark numbers between 0 and 1000 (e.g., 0, 500, 1000, or additional benchmarks as needed, depending on the readiness of students to fill in the gaps) on the clothesline. Have students draw a number card (from 0 to 1000) and pin it in the right position on the line by referring to the benchmark numbers. Have them adjust their cards as the density of the numbers on the clothesline increases. Decreasing or eliminating the amount of benchmark numbers increases the complexity of this task.
Have students play Close, Far, or In Between. Write any three numbers on the board (e.g., 237, 384, 429), and ask students questions about them. For example:
items: Which two numbers are closest? How do you know?
Which number is closest to 400? To 300?
Name a number between 384 and 429.
Name a multiple of 10 (e.g., a number that you would reach if you were skip counting by 10s) that falls between 237 and 384.
How far apart are 429 and 500? 429 and 1000? 237 and 0?
Name an even greater number than these numbers. Name an even smaller number. Do you think these are “big numbers” or “small numbers”? Why?

tasks.text: Have students use the millimetre markings on a metre stick to compare and order numbers. Because there are multiple scales on a metre stick – and because typically the dominant scale is centimetres – this can be challenging for some students. Have students count the hash marks to notice the relationship between the centimetre markings and millimetres. Give them a few measurements, for example, 12 mm, 555 mm, 102 mm, 734 mm, and 999 mm, and have them find these on the metre stick.

keyConcepts.text: Rounding numbers is often done to estimate a quantity or measure, estimate the results of a computation, and make an estimated comparison.

How close a rounded number is to the original number depends on the unit or place value that it is being rounded to. A number rounded to the nearest ten is closer to the original number than a number being rounded to the nearest hundred.
Whether a number is rounded “up” or “down” depends on the context. For example, when paying by cash in a store, the amount owing is rounded to the nearest five cents.

In the absence of a context, numbers are typically rounded based on the midpoint. This approach involves considering the amount that is halfway between two units and determining whether a number is closer to one unit than other:

items.text: Rounding 237 to the nearest 10 becomes 240, since 237 is closer to 240 than 230.
Rounding 237 to the nearest 100 becomes 200, since 237 is closer to 200 than 300.

keyConcepts.text: If a number is exactly on the midpoint, the “half round up”, which is the common method for rounding would round up to the nearest 10. So, 235 rounded to the nearest 10 becomes 240.

tasks.text: Adapt the number line clothesline from B1.2, Sample Task 1 by hanging numbers that are multiples of 100 as the benchmarks for rounding. Place a clothespin at the halfway mark of each benchmark section. Give students number cards with three-digit numbers, such as 128, 567, and 902. Have them decide whether their number card is on the right side or the left side of the halfway mark, explain how they know, and pin it to the nearest hundred.

To adapt this task for rounding to the nearest 10, use only a portion of the 0 to 1000 number line and include multiples of 10 as the benchmarks for rounding. For example, use the section of the line that includes 500 to 800, and give numbers such as 517, 601, and 789 for practice. Have students use desk- size open number lines to practise rounding with partners on similar tasks.

Have students imagine real-life situations where rounding could be used and support them in understanding that context matters. Create a variety of problems for them to solve, for example, how many $10 bills they would need to pay for a purchase that totals $32. Ask them to explain their thinking.

keyConcepts.text: Counting usually has a purpose, such as determining how many are in a collection, determining how long before something will happen, or comparing quantities and amounts.
A count can start from zero or any other starting number.
The unit of skip counting is identified as the number of objects in a group. For example, when counting by twos, each group has two objects.
Counting can involve a combination of skip counts and single counts.
The 0 to 9 and decade counting sequences that appear in the first hundred repeat in every subsequent hundred.

tasks.text: Have students count by ones from 196 to 230. Ensure that they notice that the 1 to 9 pattern repeats within every decade, and that the decade pattern repeats in every hundred. So that students understand that this occurs within every hundred, repeat this process between another two hundreds (e.g., counting from 596 to 630).
To support students’ recognition of how skip counting is used in real-life contexts, pose a financial literacy scenario such as the following:
items: A bank machine dispenses cash using only $20, $50, and $100 bills. What combinations of bills could total to $680? What totals could this bank machine not make?

tasks.text: Have students share the patterns they notice as they count by different denominations. See also F1.1. Have students create a class 0 to 1000 number chart using 10 hundred charts, preferably using grid chart paper. Assign small groups to each century (0–100, 100–200, and so on), and have them fill in the numbers for that century. As students create and fill in their hundred charts, support them in noticing the patterns in the sequence that make counting predictable. Have them use these patterns to continue the counting sequence from different starting points. Display all the hundreds charts in the classroom, and use them to support counting by 50s, 100s, and 200s, as well as by other units (e.g., 10s, 20s, 25s, 50s). Cover certain numbers with sticky notes, and have students discuss how they know what number is hidden.

keyConcepts.text: Any whole number can be described using the place value of its digits.
The place (or position) of a digit determines its value (place value). The 5 in 511, for example, has a value of 5 hundreds (500) and not 5.
The order of the digits makes a difference. The number 385 describes a different quantity than 853.

The digits in a number represent groups of ones, tens, hundreds, and so on. A zero in a column indicates that there are no groups of that size in the number. It serves as a placeholder, holding the other digits in their correct “place”. For example, 57 means 5 tens and 7 ones, but 507 means 5 hundreds, 0 tens, and 7 ones.

Expanded notation represents a number according to place value. For example, 987 means there are 9 groups of 100, 8 groups of 10, and 7 ones, which in expanded notation is 900 + 80 + 7 or 9 × 100 + 8 × 10 + 7 × 1.

tasks.text: Ask students in what ways the numbers 905, 509, 950, 590 are the same and in what ways they are different. Have them distinguish between the digit (e.g., 5), the number (e.g., 509), and the value of a digit in a number (5 in 509 has a value of 500).

To reinforce the differences explored in Sample Task 1, have students enter the number “four-six-seven” on a calculator. (For the purpose of this task, describe 467 as three separate digits, rather than as a number.) Ask students how they could make the 6 digit into a 0 without just deleting the existing number and entering 407 (i.e., by subtracting 60). Anticipate that there could be many who subtract 6 instead of 60, and discuss why this is incorrect. Reinforce the role of a digit’s place in determining its value. Next ask the students what they would have to do to change the number to 7. Repeat the task with other numbers.
Have students use calculators to play Number Wipe Out with a partner. Explain the rules of the game, as follows:
items: Each student enters a three-digit number on a calculator and keeps it hidden from their partner.
Player A asks for a specific digit in Player B’s number (e.g., "Can I have all your 8s?")
Player B replies with the place-value amount of the digit(s) in their number. For example:
If the number was 888, Player B would say, “You can have eight-hundred eighty- eight.”
If the number was 828, Player B would say, “You can have eight-hundred eight.”
If the number was 288, Player B would say, “You can have eighty-eight.”
If the number was 208, Player B would say, “You can have eight.”
If the number was 206, Player B would say, “Sorry, I have nothing to give you.”
Since Player B has “given” an amount to Player A, Player B subtracts that amount from their number, and Player A adds it.

Player B now guesses a different digit in Player A’s number – a number that should change after each turn. Player A subtracts the place-value amount from their calculator number and Player B adds it to their number.
Partners take turn guessing digits and adding the value to or subtracting it from their numbers.
The game is won by the player who is the first to get their calculator to read 0.
tasks.after: To highlight the relative size of each column, have students shade in 10 × 10 grid paper squares to model the number 777 and show the size of each digit in the number. As students create their models, ask them how they know they have the right size for each digit.

tasks.text: To emphasize the “times ten” relationship between neighbouring columns, ask students to figure out how much bigger one digit’s area is than another’s (e.g., how many times will the 7 shaded squares fit into the 70 shaded squares?). Support students in comparing the areas and determining how many of one area fits into another.

Draw out the idea that the 70 is 10 times as big as 7 because the unit being counted is 10 times as big. For example, 700 is 7 hundreds (700 = 7 × 10 × 10), 70 is 7 tens (70 = 7 × 10), and 7 is 7 ones (7 = 7 × 1). Connect this learning to the work with place value in B1.1 and, in particular, the work using base ten materials (Sample Tasks 2 and 3).

keyConcepts.text: Fair-sharing or equal-sharing means that quantities are shared equally. For a whole to be shared equally, it must be partitioned so that each sharer receives the same amount.

items.text: Sometimes the share is a whole number (e.g., if 4 pieces of ribbon are shared equally among 2 people, each person gets 2 pieces of ribbon).
Sometimes the share is a fractional amount (e.g., if 4 pieces of ribbon are shared equally among 8 people, each person gets one half of a ribbon).

Sometimes the share results in a whole plus a fractional amount (mixed number) (e.g., if 4 pieces of ribbon are shared equally among 3 people, each person gets 4 one thirds or 1 and one third pieces of the ribbon).

keyConcepts.text: Comparing two different sharing situations involves reviewing the relationship (ratio) between the amount to be shared and the number of sharers.

items.text: If the amounts to be shared are the same, then the greater the number of sharers, the less each sharer gets.
If the number of sharers is the same, then the greater the amount to be shared, the greater each sharer gets.
If the amounts to be shared are the same as the number of sharers, then the amount each sharer gets is the same for each situation.
16 pieces of ribbon are shared:
between 2 friends: 16 pieces of ribbon 2 friends 8 each
between 3 friends: 16 pieces of ribbon 3 friends 5 and one third each
between 6 friends: 16 pieces of ribbon 6 friends 2 and two thirds each

tasks.text: Pose (or have students pose) a variety of equal-sharing problems that involve 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, and 10 sharers. The following are examples:
items: If 16 waffles are shared equally between 5 friends, how many waffles does each friend get? (Each friend gets 3 and one fifth waffles.)
If 10 friends want to share 15 samosas so that each friend gets the same amount, how much does each friend get? (Each friend gets 1 and five tenths or 1 and a half samosas.)

For a craft, 10 students need to share 18 pieces of string. If the students share the string equally, how much string does each student get? (Each student gets 1 and eight tenths, or 1 and four fifths pieces of string.)

tasks.text: Have students model the situation(s) with a drawing, and support those who would benefit from acting out the situation using strips of paper. Ask them how they decided to share the pieces that were left over. Introduce new fractions (i.e., fifths, tenths), and support students in using the language of mixed numbers and fractions to describe the result (e.g., 1 and one fifth; 2 and five sixths; 2 and three tenths). Have students compare the results from two different equal-sharing situations, where there is either a common number of sharers or a common amount to be shared, such as the following:
items: At one table, 8 friends equally share 13 granola bars. At a second table, 5 friends equally share 13 granola bars. If the granola bars are all the same size, do the friends at the first table or the second table get more granola bar? How much granola bar does each friend get at each table? (At the first table, more friends are sharing the same number of granola bars, so they will get less.)

A group of 5 students share 14 sticker strips from a package. A second group of 5 students share 13 sticker strips from the same package. Do the students in the first group or the second group get more stickers? (Each student in the first group sharing more sticker strips will have more stickers than each student in the second group sharing fewer sticker strips.)

tasks.text: Students may or may not need to represent these situations using a diagram or model to decide who gets more. Draw out key concepts about comparing quantities when the number of sharers is the same and when the amounts are the same, and model these conclusions symbolically as well as concretely 13 13 (e.g., 13 one eighths or 13 eighths ( 8 ) of a granola bar is less than 13 one fifths or 13 fifths ( 5 ) of a 14 13 granola bar; 14 one fifths or 14 fifths ( 5 ) is more than 13 one fifths or 13 fifths ( 5 )). Have students compare two different situations, where in one of the situations either the amount to be shared is unknown or the number of sharers is unknown. The task for students is to equalize the situations, so that everyone, in both scenarios, receives the same portion. For example:
items: 2 friends are sharing 4 plums equally. How many plums should a group of 6 friends share so that each friend in both groups has the same amount? (Each friend in the first group gets 2 plums, so the group of 6 must share 12 plums.)

A group of 6 students shares 3 m of ribbon. How many metres of ribbon should a group of 4 students share so each student in both groups gets the same amount of ribbon? (Each student in the first group gets one half of a metre of ribbon, so the group of 4 students must share 2 m of ribbon.)

14 apples are shared by 10 friends sitting at a table. How many friends need to sit at a table where there are 7 apples so that each friend at both tables gets the same amount of apple? (Half the number of apples are needed for half the number of friends, so 7 apples will serve 5 friends.)

A group of 3 students shares 2 blocks of clay equally. How many blocks of clay should a group of 6 students share so each student in both groups has the same amount of clay? (Each student in the first group gets two thirds of a block of clay, so the group of 6 students must share 4 blocks of clay.)

tasks.text: Have students model these situations with drawings, counters, paper strips, or whatever else they choose. Some students may choose to act out the situation in order to get a sense of the actions and quantities involved.
Extend the numbers in these situations (e.g., number of sharers and amount to be shared) so that students can see what other equal-sharing combinations are possible).

Draw out the constant relationships (ratio) between the numbers of sharers and the quantities, and have students describe these using multiplication and division (e.g., there are twice as many sharers, so there must be twice as much to share if the portions are to be equal). Model writing the equivalent 3 1 14 7 portions as fractions ( 6 = 2 ; 10 = 5 ) and connect to the learning in B1.7.

keyConcepts.text: When something is shared fairly or equally as five pieces, each piece is 1 one fifth of the original amount. Five one fifths make up a whole.
When something is shared fairly or equally as ten pieces, each piece is 1 one tenth of the original amount. Ten one tenths make up a whole.
Fractions are equivalent when they represent the same value or quantity.

If the original amount is shared as five pieces or ten pieces, the fractions one fifth and 2 one tenths (two tenths) are equivalent. Similarly 2 one fifths (two fifths) and 4 one tenths (four tenths) are equivalent, 3 one fifths (three fifths) and 6 one tenths (six tenths) are equivalent, 4 one fifths (four fifths) and 8 one tenths (eight tenths) are equivalent, and 5 one tenths (five fifths), and 10 one tenths (ten tenths) are equivalent.
Different fractions can describe the same amount. Five tenths, four eighths, three sixths, and two fourths all represent the same amount as one half.

Each friend splits their piece into 2 equal pieces, creating 10 equal pieces of flatbread. The one fifth that each friend has becomes two tenths (2 one tenths) that can be shared equally with another friend: Each pair gets two tenths of the flatbread.

items: ___ people want to share ___ arepas equally.
How much does each person receive? Describe the quantity using two different fractions.

tasks.text: By using fraction combinations such as the following, students naturally encounter equivalent fractions:
items: 2 shared by 8 (produces two eighths or one fourth)
2 shared by 6 (produces two sixths or one third)

tasks.after: As with B1.6, encourage students to model the situation with a drawing or act it out using strips of paper. Have students discuss their different but equivalent answers. Support them in thinking about the patterns that make fractions equivalent (e.g., the “times two” pattern in “one fourth makes two eighths”, “one third makes two sixths”, “one fifth makes two tenths"), and model students’ thinking by writing the fractions symbolically in order to make explicit the ways in which these fractions are related. See B1.6, Sample Task 3 for examples that require equalizing two different sharing situations. Draw out the relationships between the equivalent fractions that represent the two situations.

keyConcepts.text: Multiplication and division can describe situations involving repeated groups of equal size:

items.text: Multiplication names the unknown total when the number of groups and the size of the groups are known.
Division names either the number of groups or the size of the groups when only one is known along with the total.

keyConcepts.text: Multiplication and division are inverse operations. (See B2.2, B2.6, and B2.7.)

Any division question can be thought of as a multiplication question unless 0 is involved (e.g., 16 ÷ 2 = ? is the same as ? × 2 = 16), and vice versa. This inverse relationship can be used to perform and check calculations.

items.text: 4 × 6 represented using ten frames: 4 × 6 = (4 × 5) + (4 × 1) = 20 + 4 = 24

examples.text: relationship between multiplication and division: 10 ÷ 2 can be interpreted as 10 divided into two 10 ÷ 2 can be interpreted as 10 divided into groups: how much is in each group? groups of 2: how many groups?

tasks.text: Provide students with tasks that use the commutative property for multiplication. For example, have them demonstrate using tools that 4 groups of 8 objects equals the same total number of objects as 8 groups of 4 objects.

Have students use a rekenrek to model multiplication involving equal-sized groups of beads using their known facts for 5 and adding one or two more groups. For example, 6 x 4 is the same as 4 rows of 5 beads on the rekenrek plus 4 rows of 1 bead: To reinforce the inverse relationship between multiplication and division, draw on the learning from the sample tasks in B2.6 and B2.7 and the drawings students have created to represent those situations. Highlight how the diagrams could show, for example, 3 × 5 = 15 and 15 ÷ 3 = 5. Discuss how this relationship could be used to check that a calculation is correct.

Have students adapt the memory card game described in B2.2, Sample Task 3 to reinforce the relationship between multiplication and division when learning facts. Students turn over three cards, aiming to match the facts to the representation, and when they find three that match, they say the product and quotient and keep the trio of cards. Support students in noticing how and why the same representation can show both multiplication and division, and reinforce the inverse relationship.

keyConcepts.text: Multiplication and division are inverse operations, and the basic facts for division can be rephrased using multiplication (see B2.1). For example, 16 ÷ 2 can be rewritten as ? × 2 = 16, and thought of as “how many groups of 2 are in 16?” (i.e., grouping division).

a corresponding drawing or representation (e.g., an array or number line)

keyConcepts.text: Mental math refers to doing a calculation in one’s head. Sometimes the numbers or the number of steps in a calculation are too complex to completely hold in one’s head, so jotting down partial calculations and diagrams are can be used to complete the calculations.
Number lines, circular number lines, and part-whole models can be used to show strategies for doing the calculations.
Estimation by rounding (see B1.3) is a useful mental strategy when either an exact answer is not needed or there is insufficient time to work out a solution.

tasks.text: To support and strengthen mental math skills, engage students in Number Talks, including ones that involve everyday situations that are engaging to students. Ask students what strategies they could use to mentally calculate 398 + 123. Encourage them to jot down partial sums or differences that they cannot keep completely in their head. Once they have had time to think about this individually, have them share their strategies with the class. For 398 + 123, students might use some of these strategies:
items: Add the hundreds (300 + 100), add the tens (90 + 20), add the ones (8 + 3), and then combine (400 + 110 + 11).
Add the hundreds onto the largest number (398 + 100), and then count on the tens and the ones (498 + 20 + 3) in any order.
Work with friendlier numbers and adjust (400 + 123 = 523, so 398 + 123 is two less).
Estimate the solution (398 + 123 ≈ 400 + 120).

tasks.text: Ask students to mentally subtract 137 from 452, jotting down partial sums or differences that they cannot keep entirely in their heads. After giving them individual think time, have them share their strategies with the class and assist them in making connections to place value, basic facts, and relationships between numbers and operations. Use a number line to communicate strategies visually, and support students in moving towards increasingly efficient strategies as they are ready. For 452 − 137, students might do the following:
items: Think using addition (452 − 137 can be represented as 137 + ? = 452) and count on to reach the total, for example, add 300 to 137 to get 437, then add 3 to get 440, then add 12 to get 452, so the answer is 315.
Subtract the hundreds first (452 – 100 = 352), then the tens (352 – 30 = 322), and then the ones (322 – 7 = 315).
Use friendlier numbers and adjust (452 − 140 is 312, so 452 − 137 is three more).
Create a friendlier question by keeping the difference constant (452 − 137 is the same difference as 455 − 140).

keyConcepts.text: The most common standard algorithms for addition and subtraction in North America use a very compact organizer to decompose and recompose numbers based on place value (see B1.1 and B1.5).

items.text: The North American algorithms for addition and subtraction both start from the right and move to the left, digit by digit.
The digits in the unit column are added or subtracted.
When the sum of two digits exceeds 9 or the difference is below zero, a “regroup” or a “trade” (decomposing and recomposing) from the next column is made so that the operation can be carried out.
The process is repeated for every column and small numbers are used to track and manage the regroupings.

keyConcepts.text: One way to model multiplication and division is to use repeated groups of equal size.
Multiplication and division are related. A division problem can be thought of as a multiplication problem with a missing factor (unless 0 is involved). So 24 ÷ 6 can be rewritten as 6 × ? = 24.
The array can be a very useful model for multiplication and division because it structures repeated groups of equal size into rows and columns.

items.text: In a multiplication situation the number of rows and the number of columns for the array are both known.

In a division situation the total number of objects is known, as well as either the number of rows or the number of columns. In order to create an array to represent a division situation, the objects are arranged into the rows or columns that are known until all the objects have been distributed evenly.

keyConcepts.text: Multiplication and division are both useful for describing situations involving repeated groups of equal size.

items.text: Multiplication names the unknown total when the number of groups and the size of the groups are known.
Division names either the unknown size of groups (sharing division), or the unknown number of groups (grouping division) when the total is known.

keyConcepts.text: The inverse relationship between multiplication and division means that any situation involving repeated equal groups can be represented with either multiplication or division. See also B2.1.
There are two types of division problems:

items.text: Equal-sharing division (also called “partitive division”):
What is known: the total and number of groups.
What is unknown: the size of the groups.
The action: a total shared equally among a given number of groups. (See B1.6 and B1.7 for connections between equal-sharing division and fractions.)

keyConcepts.text: Equal-grouping division (sometimes called “measurement division” or “quotative division”):

items.text: What is known: the total and the size of groups.
What is unknown: the number of groups.
The action: from a total, equal groups of a given size are measured out.

keyConcepts.text: Repeated addition and repeated subtraction are often used as strategies to solve multiplication and division problems.
Repeated addition is often used as a multiplication strategy, by adding equal groups to find the total.

Repeated addition is also often used as a division strategy, by thinking of the division as multiplication with a missing factor (e.g., thinking of 15 ÷ 3 as 3 × ? = 15 and asking how many groups of 3 are in 15).

Repeated subtraction is often used as a division strategy, by removing equal groups from the given total. Each round of sharing is “unitized” as a group and subtracted from the total. Each repeated round is represented as a subtracted group.

keyConcepts.text: Patterns can be extended because they are repetitive by nature.
Pattern rules are generalizations about a pattern, and they can be described in words.
Patterns can be extended in multiple directions – up, down, right, left, diagonally.

To make a near prediction about a pattern is to state or show what a pattern will look like just beyond the given representation of that pattern. The prediction can be verified by extending the pattern.

To make a far prediction about a pattern is to state or show what a pattern will look like well beyond the given representation of that pattern. Often calculations are needed to make an informed prediction or to verify a prediction.
To identify missing elements of patterns is to complete a representation for a given pattern by filling in the missing parts.

Have them describe that visual in words so that they notice the numbers that are being combined to create the equivalent representations, for example, three sets of 4-rods and four sets of 3-rods. When students are adding or multiplying whole numbers, have them show the equivalence using the commutative property and ask them to describe how the expressions are equivalent.

Ask students to represent a number such as 12 with relational rods. Then, ask them to represent that same number using multiplication, in more than one way, and label each representation using symbols. When students are adding whole numbers, have them demonstrate equivalence using the commutative property of addition, for example 8 + 352 = 352 + 8, and ask them to describe how the expressions are equivalent. They should also be encouraged to use the commutative property of multiplication, for example 5 × 2 = 2 × 5. In a similar way, have them demonstrate equivalence using the associative and commutative properties of addition. For example, 263 + 364 + 7 is the same as 263 + 7 + 364. Students are not expected to be able to name or define these properties, but they should be able to use them appropriately.

tasks.text: Coding can be simplified to include a loop for repeating the same set of instructions a given number of times. Have students use loops to support their understanding of mathematical concepts that involve repetitive or iterative tasks. For example, the construction of a square is a repeat of the same length, four times, with a right-angle turn between repeats. Have students create a program that instructs an agent (e.g., digital image, robot, classmate) to move in the shape of a square. They can explore writing the code with and without loops to compare the two approaches. This type of activity can reinforce properties of shapes and patterns.

A repeat or a loop can also be used to repeat operations. For example, have students create code that has them state a starting number and then repeatedly add on or take away from that number. This type of activity can support students in making connections between counting and numerical patterns.

keyConcepts.text: Code can be altered to develop students’ understanding of mathematical concepts, and to ensure that the code is generating the expected outcome.
Altering code to use loops can simplify instructions while generating the same outcome.
The placement of a loop in the code can affect the outcome.
Changing the sequence of instructions in code can sometimes produce the same outcome and can sometimes produce a different outcome.

keyConcepts.text: Data can be sorted in more than one way.
Two-way tables are used to sort data into all of the possible combinations for the characteristics of two attributes.
A three-circle Venn diagram can be used to sort data based on three characteristics (e.g., red, large, stripes) for three attributes (e.g., colour, size, markings).
A Carroll diagram can be used to sort data into complementary sets for two characteristics (e.g., red – not red, stripes – no stripes) for two attributes (e.g., colour, markings).

A tree diagram can be used to sort data into all the possible combinations of characteristics for two or more attributes (e.g., red stripes, red dots, blue stripes, blue dots, green stripes, green dots).

When students are first learning about “mean” as it relates to data, it might be helpful to support them in understanding the idea by talking about “levelling out” or redistributing the data. For example, Student A has 6 markers, Student B has 4 markers, and Student C has 5 markers. To find the mean for the number of markers, the quantities must be “levelled out” or redistributed so that each student has 5 markers, which is the mean.

tasks.text: Have students identify the mode(s), if any, for a variety of data sets. For example, give students a set that has one number appearing more than any other, a set that has two or more numbers appearing more than any other, a set in which all the numbers appear the same number of times, and a set where all the numbers are different.

In this early work with mean, it is important that the data sets students work with be represented with concrete materials only and contain only small numbers that can easily be manipulated. This enables students to learn concretely – to manipulate the numbers using concrete tools until the numbers in all the categories are the same.
Start with a scenario where three students have three different numbers of cubes: 3, 2, and 1. Ask “What do we need to do so that everyone has the same number of cubes?”
Repeat with 4, 3, and 2 cubes; then with 5, 3, and 1 cubes; and so on.

Have students determine the mean for a data set of 6, 3, 3, 2, and 1 using a concrete graph. To groups of 5 students, distribute rods of 6, 3, 3, 2, and 1 interlocking cubes. Ask students to imagine that this is the number of pieces of fruit in all their lunches. Ask them to organize the rods in ascending order and to find the mode. Now ask them to redistribute the cubes so that everyone has the same number. This represents the mean or average number of pieces of fruit that each student had in their lunch. Ask whether every student had three pieces of fruit (in reality, some may have had more, some may have had fewer, and some may have had three). Through these kinds of activities, students will begin to develop a conceptual understanding of the idea of central distribution.

keyConcepts.text: Different representations are used for different purposes to convey different types of information.
Frequency tables show numerically how often an item or value occurs in a set of data. They are quicker and easier to read than tallies.

Graphs of quantitative data show the distribution and the shape of the data. For example, the data on a vertical bar graph may be skewed to the left, skewed to the right, centred, or equally distributed among all of the categories.

It is important to pay attention to the scale on pictographs and other graphs. If the scale on a pictograph is that one picture represents two students, then the frequency of a category is double what is shown.
Data that is presented in tables and graphs can be used to ask and answer questions, draw conclusions, and make convincing arguments and informed decisions.

Questions of interest are intended to be answered through the analysis of the representations. Sometimes the analysis raises more questions that require further collection, representation, and analysis of data.

keyConcepts.text: Three-dimensional objects have attributes that allow them to be identified, compared, sorted, and classified.

Geometric properties are attributes that are the same for an entire group of three-dimensional objects. Some attributes are relevant for classifying objects by geometry. Others are not. For example, colour and size are attributes but are not relevant for geometry since there are large cubes, small cubes, blue cubes, and yellow cubes. Having six congruent faces, where each face is a square, is an attribute and a geometric property because all cubes, by definition, have this property.
When sorting and building objects, some of the attributes that are useful to name and notice are the number and shape of the faces, the number of edges, and the number of vertices and angles.

When three-dimensional objects are sorted by geometric properties or categories, classes emerge. Each class of three-dimensional object has common geometric properties, and these properties are unaffected by the size or orientation of an object.

tasks.text: Provide students with nets for a cube, a prism, a pyramid, a cylinder, and a cone as well as a labelled picture of each. Ask them to predict which three-dimensional object each of the nets will form. Next, have them construct shapes from the nets to verify their predictions. Ask them to identify the two- dimensional shapes that make up each of the three-dimensional objects they have built. Discuss the geometric properties (including the number of faces, edges, vertices, and angles) of each of these three- dimensional objects.

Have students, in small groups, make pairs of cards for cubes, prisms, pyramids, cylinders, and cones. On one card have them draw or glue a picture of the three-dimensional object, and on the other card they write its name. Once they are finished, have them shuffle the cards and lay them face down in rows and columns. They can then play “Concentration”, taking turns flipping two cards up and trying to match the picture of the three-dimensional object with its name.

Have students play “What’s My Name?”. Working in pairs, students choose a secret three-dimensional object (e.g., a triangle-based prism) and write down everything that is “interesting” about this object, using the language of geometric properties (including the number of faces, edges, vertices, and angles). Pairs then use this information to write a series of clues. Each pair listens to another pair’s clues, guesses the name of the secret object, and explains their reasoning. A variation of this task is to have students play “Twenty Questions” using a series of yes-no questions to determine the mystery object.

keyConcepts.text: Structures are composed of three-dimensional objects with faces that are two-dimensional shapes. Recognizing and describing the shapes and objects in three-dimensional structures provides insight into how structures are built.
Objects and structures can be decomposed physically and visually (e.g., using the “mind’s eye”). Visualization is an important skill to develop.

Triangles are useful for strengthening and stabilizing a structure; rectangular prisms are commonly used because of their ability to be stacked. This expectation is closely related to learning in the Grade 3 Structures and Mechanisms strand of the Science and Technology curriculum, 2022.

tasks.text: Have students collect images of different structures, both in natural and engineered contexts (e.g., bees’ nest, beaver dam, CN Tower, pyramid, teepee, tent, bridge, fence). Have them identify the shapes used in these constructions. This is also an opportunity to discuss the cultural, societal, and ecological significance and histories of these structures.

In conjunction with learning in the science and technology curriculum, have students describe ways to improve a structure’s strength and identify the role of struts and ties in structures that must bear a load. Have them build a bridge that can span a given distance and hold a given mass using only paper, tape, and scissors. Ask which of the structures supported the greatest mass and what features made them the strongest. Alternatively, have students experiment to find the tallest stable tower they can build using similar materials.

keyConcepts.text: Congruence is a relationship between three-dimensional objects that have the same shape and the same size. Congruent three-dimensional shapes match every face exactly, in the exact same position.
Checking for congruence is closely related to measurement. Side lengths and angles can be directly compared by matching them, one against the other. They can also be measured.

Two objects that are not congruent can still have specific elements that are congruent. For example, two objects might have a face that is congruent (i.e., the face is the same size and shape), but if the other faces are different in any way (e.g., the faces have different angles or side lengths), then the two objects are not congruent. Likewise, even if all faces are congruent but they are in a different arrangement, the two objects would not be congruent because they would not be the exact same shape.

tasks.text: Provide students with different sizes of prisms and pyramids. Ask them to compare the prisms and identify the prisms that have congruent lengths, congruent angles, and congruent faces. Then, ask students to compare the pyramids in a similar way. Have them explain their strategies for determining congruence.

Make a structure with four interlocking cubes, and ask students to use four interlocking cubes to make a structure congruent to the first. Next, ask them to use their four cubes to build as many unique structures as they can. Tell them to verify that each is unique by flipping and turning it. They should work to build all six of the possible structures that can be made with four interlocking cubes. This task can be extended to structures made using five cubes and six cubes.

keyConcepts.text: Instructions to move from one location to another location require information about direction and distance from a given location.

items.text: Numbers and units describe distance (e.g., 5 steps; 3 kilometres).

Absolute direction can be conveyed using cardinal language (i.e., N, S, E, W), which was introduced in Grade 2 to locate selected communities, countries, and/or continents on a map (See The Ontario Curriculum: Social Studies, Grades 1 to 6; History and Geography, Grades 7 and 8, 2018, Grade 2, B3.3).
Relative direction can be conveyed using qualitative language (right, left, forward, backward, up, down).
Relative direction can be quantified and made more precise by describing the amount of turn.

keyConcepts.text: The amount of a turn involves the measure of angles, a skill that is more formally developed in Grades 4 and 5. In Grade 3, the language of half- and quarter-turn parallels the minute hand of an analog clock. A turn may be clockwise (moving in the same direction as the hands of a clock) or counterclockwise (the opposite direction from the hands of a clock).

items.text: A full turn is a full circle that results in an object facing in the same direction (e.g., start at 12 o’clock, end at 12 o’clock). A full turn clockwise or counterclockwise produces the same result.
A half-turn results in an object facing the opposite direction, (e.g., start at 12 o’clock, end at 6 o’clock). A half-turn clockwise or counterclockwise produces the same result.

A quarter-turn results in an object facing either 9 o’clock or 3 o’clock, (i.e., start at 12 o’clock, and go a quarter-turn clockwise, and end at 3 o’clock, or go a quarter-turn counterclockwise, and end at 9 o’clock).

tasks.text: Have students identify a game that is relevant to them and describe the rules for moving game pieces, using the language of distance and turns. For example, in the game of chess, a knight moves in an L shape. It can move two squares horizontally and then one square vertically, or it could move two squares vertically and then one square horizontally. Have students teach their instructions to others who do not know the game, and then play it with them. Alternatively, they could invent their own game using these same movements and play it with others in the class.

Have students write code for a classmate (or small robot or digital image) to move from one location to another, with instructions related to distances and turns. This task may also involve the classmate creating a shape or a pattern.

Have students write instructions for finding a hidden object in the classroom using cardinal directions and length measurements (metric and/or non-standard units). Support them in testing the accuracy of the instructions with their peers and adjusting as needed. As an extension, add vertical directions (up and down) to find hidden objects that are not at ground level.

keyConcepts.text: Perimeter is the total length or distance around an object or region. A perimeter measurement is a length measurement.
If a perimeter is made up of straight lines, the parts are measured with a ruler and the measurements are combined. This is an application of the additivity property.

Curved perimeters are difficult to measure accurately with a ruler. A “go-between”, like a string, is used to match the perimeter of the object and then measured. The measurement of the go- between is used as the measurement of the perimeter. This is an application of the transitivity property.

Different shapes can have the same perimeter. A shape with a perimeter of 20 centimetres could be a 5 centimetres × 5 centimetres square, a skinny rectangle that is 2 centimetres × 8 centimetres, any other polygon, a combination of curves and straight lines, or a completely curved shape. To construct a shape with a given perimeter, the amount of length must always be tracked so that the remaining length can be distributed appropriately around the rest of the shape.

Measurements of continuous quantities, like length, are always approximate. The smaller the unit, the greater the potential accuracy. If different-sized units are used to measure an object, each unit is counted and tracked separately.

Because measurements are approximate, a combination of units might be used for greater accuracy (e.g., a combination of centimetres and millimetres for a length between 5 centimetres and 6 centimetres).

The appropriate unit of length depends on the reason for measuring an object. Larger units are used for approximate measurements; smaller units are used for precise measurements and detailed work. While non-standard units are appropriate for quick, personal measurements, standard units are used when communicating measurements.

tasks.text: Have students construct shapes with a perimeter of 18 units on a geoboard or grid paper, noting that diagonal sides are not permitted. Ask them to determine the shape with the fewest sides and the shape with the most sides. Discuss how they might draw curved shapes with the same perimeter (e.g., using a string), and support them in recognizing that there are an infinite number of possible shapes with a perimeter of 18 units.

keyConcepts.text: Millimetres, centimetres, metres, and kilometres are standard metric units of length. The metre is the metric standard or base unit of length.

items.text: 1 metre is equal to 100 centimetres or 1000 millimetres.
1000 metres is equal to 1 kilometre.

keyConcepts.text: For convenience, there are symbols for metric units: millimetre (mm), centimetre (cm), metre (m), kilometre (km).

Standard and non-standard units are equally accurate (provided that the measurement itself is carried out well). However, standard units allow people to communicate distances and lengths with others in ways that are consistently understood. Metric units are the standard for all but three countries in the world and are the focus of this expectation.
The metric system is universally used by scientists because it uses standard prefixes which helps in the understanding of measurements and conversions.

tasks.text: Have students identify the markings for millimetres and centimetres on a metre stick. Using the metre stick as a reference, ask them to identify the number of millimetres in one centimetre, the number of centimetres in one metre, and the number of millimetres in one metre. Ask them to identify a real-life object or personal referent (benchmark) that could be less than 1 cm, approximately 1 cm, and approximately 1 m. Next, have them estimate the length of another object or a distance using those benchmarks. Have them verify their estimates by measuring.

Provide students with an example of a well-known location (e.g., the community garden) that is 1 km from their school. Then provide them with other examples of well-known locations (e.g., the local library, the nearest park), and ask if they think they are more or less than 1 km away.
If weather and safety permit, take a 1 km stroll with students so that they get a sense of how far 1 km is and how long it takes them to move that distance.

Have students choose the most appropriate standard unit (millimetre, centimetre, metre, kilometre) in a given situation and explain their reasoning (e.g., “I would measure the distance to Sandbanks Provincial Park in kilometres because it is a long way away, and kilometres are much larger than centimetres and metres.”). Support students in recognizing that using smaller units produces greater accuracy, and that choosing appropriate units involves determining what level of accuracy is required.

keyConcepts.text: Capacity is the amount a container can hold. It can be directly compared by pouring the contents of one container into another.

Similar to measuring length, capacity can be quantified and measured by determining how many equal-sized units something holds. Using units supports moving from comparison questions (Which holds more?) to measurement questions (How much? How much more?).
To directly measure the capacity of an object:

tasks.text: Show students two different-sized containers (e.g., margarine tub, cottage cheese container, food storage container). [Have enough for the the entire class, working in pairs]. Explain the following situation to them:
items: I usually have soup for lunch. Today, I forgot to bring a soup bowl to school. I found these two containers that I could use instead. I want to use the container that will hold the most soup. Which container do you think has the greater capacity?

tasks.text: Ask them to work with a partner to determine which of the two containers should be used for the lunch. Provide a variety of tools (e.g., coffee scoops, small plastic cups) and materials (e.g., centicubes, marbles, cotton balls) for them to use to determine the capacity of each of the containers. After students have carried out their investigation, compare and discuss their findings. Draw out important considerations, such as the importance of filling and levelling each scoopful in order to measure accurately, and how some materials fill in more space than others, resulting in a more (or less) accurate measurement.

Have students compare the capacity of several small rectangular boxes. Have them predict the order of the boxes from least capacity to greatest capacity. Then have them check their prediction by filling the boxes with solid objects of the same size (e.g., balls, blocks, interlocking cubes, marbles, sand). Ask them to identify which objects resulted in the biggest gaps when filling the containers, and which resulted in the smallest gaps. Then discuss which objects provided a more accurate and a less accurate measure of the capacities.

keyConcepts.text: Mass is the amount of matter in an object. Objects with more mass have more weight.

Although the weight of an object may vary in different locations, its mass is constant. For example, the weight of an object on Jupiter is more than it is on Earth because weight is affected by gravity, but the mass of the object is the same in both places.

Mass is quantified and measured by using units of mass and finding out how many units it takes to match the mass of the object. Any collection of uniform objects with the same amount of mass can serve as a unit of mass. Units enable a move from comparison questions (Which is heavier?) to measurement questions (How much heavier?).
Two-pan balance scales or spring scales are used to indirectly compare and measure the mass of an object.

items.text: Before measuring, ensure that the two pans on the balance are “balanced” or the spring scale is set to start at zero. This is equivalent to eliminating gaps or overlaps when measuring other attributes.
For a balance scale, place the object on one pan and add units of mass to the other pan until the two pans balance.

For spring scales, place the object on the spring scale and record the distance the spring scale moves; remove the object and replace it with just enough units of mass to pull the spring down the same distance.
Count how many units it takes to match the object.

keyConcepts.text: If different-sized units are used to match an object’s mass more exactly, each unit is counted and tracked separately. For example, if 5 small washers equal 1 large washer, then 2 large 3 washers and 3 small washers could be written as 25 large washers.

keyConcepts.text: Measurement is more than a count; it is a spatial comparison. Units enable a spatial comparison to be quantified.

How much length, mass, area, or capacity an object has remains constant unless the object itself has been changed (conservation principle). An amount is not changed by measuring with different units; only the count of units changes. Using smaller units produces a greater count than using larger units (inverse relationship).

items.text: length: measuring the same distance between two points using metres, centimetres, and millimetres
perimeter: measuring the distance around an object using metres, centimetres, and millimetres
area: covering a rectangular space using different sizes of rectangles
capacity: filling a container using a full cup, half a cup, and a quarter of a cup
mass: measuring the mass of an object using different sizes of washers

tasks.text: Show students two lines of different lengths, arranged at different angles so they are not easily compared visually. Ask: “Which line is longer?” Students verify their selection by choosing a unit to measure the two lines. After they have used the count of units to verify which line is longer (e.g., “This line is longer because it is 10 paper clips long and the other is 9 paper clips long.”), have them replace the units used to measure the shorter line with a smaller unit, so that the shorter line now produces a greater count (e.g., the length that was 9 paper clips long is now 12 cubes long). Ask students how long each line is now, and which line is longer. Support students who are mistakenly distracted by the count (e.g., “This one is longer because it has 12.”) by helping them recognize that, since the line did not change, neither did the length. Focus attention on the role of the unit in comparing measurements, and support students in noticing that smaller units will produce larger counts.

Variations of Sample Task 1 could be done using mass or capacity. For example, students might measure the mass of two objects with the same unit of mass to determine which is heavier, then measure the lightest object again using a lighter unit of mass, thereby generating a greater count. Alternatively, after measuring the capacity of two containers, students could use a larger unit of capacity to measure the larger container, thereby generating a smaller count.

Have students cover a rectangular surface with two or more different sizes of rectangles to be used as the unit of measure (e.g., recipe cards, paper, sticky notes). Ask them to place the rectangles close to each other with no overlaps or gaps. Have them compare the number of each type of unit of measure needed to cover the surface. Identify the unit of measure that requires the least number of counts, and the unit of measure that requires the greatest number of counts.

keyConcepts.text: Clocks can answer two questions: “What time is it?” and “How much time has passed?”. The focus in Grade 3 is on the first question.

A colon (:) is used to separate units of time. Generally, time is read in hours and minutes, so 12:36 means 36 minutes after 12:00. To describe time more precisely, another colon is used to show seconds, so 12:36:15 means it is 15 seconds after 12:36.
Analog clocks use fractions of a circle to provide benchmark times: quarter past the hour; half past the hour; and quarter to the hour. Benchmark times are not evident in digital clocks.
Analog clocks have a face with three different scales. Navigating these scales can make reading an analog clock challenging.

items.text: The shorter hour hand (0 to 12, numbered scale) measures broad approximate time.
The longer minute hand (0 to 60, unnumbered markings) measures time more precisely.
The optional second hand (same 0 to 60 scale as that used by the minute hand) is used for precise time.

keyConcepts.text: The 24-hour clock is widely used in transportation schedules and in the military. For many parts of the world, it is the standard way of describing time.

tasks.text: To help students understand the two (or three) different scales on a clock, take the minute hand (and second hand, if there is one) off a working clock, and use only the hour hand to tell time. Have students use the language of approximation to describe time related to the hour (e.g., about 2 o’clock; just before noon; just after 10 o’clock; halfway between 1 o’clock and 2 o’clock). Keep the clock on display for a period of time, and occasionally ask students to describe what time it is. Ask them to notice the placement of the (hour) hand depending on the time; for example, if it is half past one, the hand is halfway between the 1 and the 2. If it is 11 o’clock, the hand is on the 11.

Over time and after enough practice that students are comfortable working with the hour hand, introduce the minute hand of the clock and what happens to it as the hour hand goes from one hour to the next. For example, if the hour hand is halfway between two numbers, where is the minute hand? This will begin to develop students’ understanding of the benchmark of half past the hour. Similarly, if the hour hand is just past or before an hour, where is the minute hand? This will begin to develop benchmarks for 10 and 15 minutes past or before the hour.

Occasionally ask students approximately what time it is on the one-handed clock, and ask them to predict where the minute hand would be. Verify by checking a two-handed clock (which could be hidden from their view).

To further support work with the minute-hand scale, have students build five-cube lengths to represent the 5-minute intervals between the numbers on the analog clock (as shown in the diagram) and to emphasize that there are 60 minutes in each hour. The numbers inside the "dial" represent hours, while the numbers outside the dial represent minutes.
Have students use digital clocks alongside analog clocks to create opportunities to express minutes in relation to fractional benchmarks:
items: 15 minutes is one quarter of an hour. On an analog clock, the minute hand on the 3 shows 15 minutes. Why is that?
30 minutes is one half of an hour. On an analog clock, the minute hand on the 6 shows 30 minutes. Why is that?
45 minutes is three quarters of an hour. On an analog clock, the minute hand on the 9 shows 45 minutes. Why is that?

tasks.text: Have students use digital and analog clocks to read and record meaningful times throughout the day. Depending on the interests of students, a follow-up activity could be to explore other ways to communicate the time, such as “It is twenty to two.”

Introduce students to the 24-hour clock and how it is used in everyday life (e.g., bus schedules, train schedules, airline schedules, military time, in hospital settings), and discuss why this might be a good format to use. Have them use a double number line (0 to 24 above; 1 a.m. to 12 noon and 1 p.m. to 12 midnight below) to observe relationships to the 12-hour clock. Discuss how addition and subtraction (adding or subtracting 12 to or from the hour) can help them move between the two conventions for telling time.

keyConcepts.text: Area is the amount of surface or space inside a two-dimensional region. An area can be directly compared to another area by covering and matching the areas to determine which is larger.
The same area can take the form of an infinite number of shapes.
To better compare two areas, an area can be decomposed and “re-shaped” to make covering and matching easier. If the amount of an area doesn’t change, the comparison is valid.

tasks.text: Provide pairs of students with several rectangular cards of the same size. Ask them to cut the cards along their diagonals and rearrange the resulting two triangles into different shapes – the only rule being that only equal side lengths can be joined. Ask them to find all the different possibilities and record the combinations. Have students discuss whether the areas of these different shapes are the same or different, and have them share their reasoning.

Provide students with outlines of composite shapes made using tangram pieces. Have them visually compare the outlines and decide whether the areas are the same, then check their prediction by using tangram pieces to fill in the outlines. Ask them whether their predictions were correct, and have them provide evidence of their thinking.

keyConcepts.text: Units quantify comparisons and are used to change comparison questions (Which is takes up more space?) into measurement questions (How much area does this shape have? Which shape has more area?). A unit of area is used to measure area.
A unit of area is an amount of area. It is not a shape. Two different shapes, if they have the same area, can represent the same unit.
Area is measured by counting how many units of area it takes to cover (tile) a surface without gaps or overlaps.
Gaps between units produce an underestimate, and overlaps produce an overestimate. Both affect the accuracy of the count.
Units of area can be decomposed, rearranged, and redistributed to better cover an area and minimize gaps or overlaps. If the amount of area is preserved, the unit is constant, regardless of its form.
Choosing an appropriate object or shape to represent a unit of area is an important decision when measuring area. The object must:

have a constant area;
be able to be decomposed and rearranged as necessary.

tasks.text: Provide students with a “messy math box”, filled with objects that may or may not be appropriate for measuring area (e.g., paper squares, grid paper, square tiles, marbles, cotton balls, circular tiles). Have them select objects to use to measure the areas of a variety of polygons. Support them in defining the criteria for what makes an object more appropriate than others to use as a unit to measure area (e.g., the objects are the same size and easily tiled with no gaps or overlaps).

Have students select objects to use to measure the area of a variety of curved shapes. Guide them to understand that the object being used to measure can be reshaped, or decomposed and rearranged, to fill the area of the curved shape (e.g., paper squares can be cut into smaller parts). Add this to the criteria identified in Sample Task 1.

keyConcepts.text: Squares tile a grid without gaps or overlaps and are the conventional shape used to describe units of area. A square with a side length of 1 unit (i.e., a unit square) has 1 square unit of area. Any standard unit of length (i.e., metric or imperial) can produce a standard unit of area.
Square centimetres and square metres are standard metric units of area.

items.text: A square with dimensions 1 cm × 1 cm has an area of one square centimetre (1 cm2).
A square with dimensions 1 m × 1 m has an area of 1 square metre (1 m2).
Square centimetres and square metres are amounts of area. Although their definitions are based on squares, they can come in any shape.

keyConcepts.text: Area is measured by counting the number of full or partial units needed to cover a surface. For example, a surface that is completely covered by 18 unit squares has an area of 18 square units.

tasks.text: Show students a 1 cm × 1 cm square. Have them estimate how many 1 cm × 1 cm squares are needed to cover a rectangular surface, such as a book. Have them verify their estimate. Based on this experience, have them estimate how many 1 cm × 1 cm squares would be needed to cover other rectangular surfaces.

Have students make a square metre (m2) out of newspaper, wrapping paper, or craft paper. Have them use their square metre model(s) to estimate and measure the area of the classroom or a hallway. To reinforce the idea that a unit of area is a quantity and not a shape, challenge students to create different “triangular” square metres and prove that they all still have an area of 1 m2.

Give students various non-rectangular shapes, including curved ones, that are transcribed onto centimetre grid paper. Have them estimate the area of these shapes by mentally recomposing partial squares to make full square units. Discuss strategies for keeping track of partial squares and estimating a total. Reinforce the idea that the unit of measure is square centimetres, and support them in using proper conventions (e.g., 24 cm2).

As an outdoor activity, assign students to work in pairs and have them trace one another’s shadows using sidewalk chalk. Have them use 10 cm × 10 cm squares of grid paper to measure the area of their shadow, in square centimetres. Have them verify that every square has an area of 100 cm2, and have them use these squares to cover their shadows and determine a count of area units. As they estimate the area of the curved sections of the shadow, support them in recognizing that they can decompose or cut the units into smaller parts and redistribute them, as long as they maintain a count of full units. Discuss strategies for keeping track of partial squares and estimating a total. After they cover the area, have them identify their area measurement using square centimetres (cm2).

tasks.text: Indicate the “price” in whole-dollar amounts for a variety of items (e.g., items in the classroom, such as a stapler, a pencil case, a notebook, or a box of crayons). Have students select three or four items to “purchase” and estimate the total cost in whole-dollar amounts.

Provide a dollar amount for students to “spend”. Ask them to add up purchases of several items and determine how much change, if any, they should receive. Use concrete or digital play money to enhance these experiences. Consider using scenarios that involve local community and school events.
